subject: How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?

messages.author: 4b4bfd4b9a38f60f
messages.subject: How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?
parts:
Hello.

I'm trying to implement a Naive Bayes model in Stan, however it seems to be very slow and eats a crazy amount of memory, and I'm wondering if I'm doing something wrong.

The code is (it's based on the example code)

// supervised naive Bayes
data {
// training data
int<lower=1> K; // num category
int<lower=1> V; // num words
int<lower=1> M; // num docs
int<lower=1> N; // number of words
int<lower=1, upper=K> s[M]; // category for doc m
int<lower=1, upper=V> w[N]; // word n
int<lower=1, upper=M> doc[N]; // doc ID for word n
//hyper params
//vector<lower=0>[K] alpha; // category prior
//vector<lower=0>[V] beta; // word prior
}
parameters {
simplex[K] theta; // category prevalence
simplex[V] phi[K]; // word dist for category k
}
model {
// priors
//theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
//for (k in 1:K)
// phi[k] ~ dirichlet(beta);
// likelihood, including latent category
for (m in 1:M)
s[m] ~ categorical(theta);
for (n in 1:N)
w[n] ~ categorical(phi[s[doc[n]]]);
}


Using the above code and a data subset with K=396 categories, V=10 different words, M=842 documents and N=23267 total words I'm getting the following:

For a single chain with 1000 samples. 

#  Elapsed Time: 402.947 seconds (Warm-up)
#                246.542 seconds (Sampling)
#                649.489 seconds (Total)

If i uncomment the priors it gets much worse (and I get much worse Rhat's)

#  Elapsed Time: 754.031 seconds (Warm-up)
#                2385.01 seconds (Sampling)
#                3139.04 seconds (Total)

This is a tiny subset of my data. When I tried to scale it up to roughly V=2000 different words it ate all my memory (16g) and crashed.

Is this kind of scalability expected?

How big Naive Bayes models can I expect to be able to fit with Stan?

In case Stan simply can't scale to data like this do you have some recommendations for other tools or techniques?

I've used scikit's NaiveBayesNB model which is lightning fast, but it's just using the MLE, and not giving you the full posterior. 

Does it make sense at all to even care about the full posterior for naive bayes?

Best, Rasmus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?
parts:
The Dirichlet is conjugate and you're using labeled data,
so the posteriors for alpha and beta will also be Dirichlet
and can be computed directly in the generated quantities block.

An intermediate step would be to collect sufficient stats
and convert the looped categorical into multinomials. That
will be a whole lot faster, but still not as fast as just
calculating the analytic posterior and drawing a sample from
that directly.

There's a discussion of doing both of these thing in the language
manual chapter on optimizing Stan code.

- Bob

parts:
To make this more concrete, here's the posterior
for theta

data {
int<lower=0> M;

And here's how you can code it directly without
using any parameters:

transformed data {
vector[K] counts;
cat_counts <- rep_vector(0, K);

cat_counts[s[m]] <- cat_counts[s[m]] + 1;
}
generated quantities {
simplex[K] theta;
theta ~ dirichlet(counts + alpha);

dirichlet(counts + alpha) is the analytic posterior here, so you
can make independent draws of theta in the generated quantities block.

The posteriors for phi all work the same way.

- Bob

I see. You're right. I can solve all this analytically.

What I'm looking for is the posterior predictive p(y|x,D) (D=data set and all the params have been integrated out), which has a closed form solution due to the conjugate priors.

I found a nice explanation of it, in case anyone else is interested: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CW9YGii1nSA

Thanks :)

 - Rasmus

On Tuesday, March 22, 2016 at 9:33:56 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
To make this more concrete, here's the posterior
for theta

data {
  int<lower=0> M;
  int<lower=1, upper=K> s[M];
  ...

model {
  ...
  theta ~ dirichlet(alpha);
  for (m in 1:M)
    s[m] ~ categorical(theta);

And here's how you can code it directly without
using any parameters:

transformed data {
  vector[K] counts;
  cat_counts <- rep_vector(0, K);
  for (m in 1:M)
    cat_counts[s[m]] <- cat_counts[s[m]] + 1;  
}
generated quantities {
  simplex[K] theta;
  theta ~ dirichlet(counts + alpha);

dirichlet(counts + alpha) is the analytic posterior here, so you
can make independent draws of theta in the generated quantities block.

The posteriors for phi all work the same way.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How scalable is Naive Bayes in Stan?
parts:
> On Mar 23, 2016, at 3:47 AM, Rasmus Berg Palm <rasmusb...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I see. You're right. I can solve all this analytically.
>

> What I'm looking for is the posterior predictive p(y|x,theta) (where theta are all the params), which seems to have a closed form solution due to the conjugate priors.

Right --- you just add the observed counts to the prior Dirichlet
parameter to get the posterior's Dirichlet parameter. The
posterior predictive for further multinomial data is then Dirichlet-multinomial:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet-multinomial_distribution

- Bob
